speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: These amendments are largely technical and operational in nature.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: The amendments fall within the following five groups.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: The first set of amendments found in Part 1 of the Bill clarifies and expands the functions and duties of the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) and the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Clause 2 amends the Building and Construction Authority Act 1999 (BCA Act) to confer the following functions on BCA.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: BCA will also take on the function of maintaining foreshore structures belonging to the Government and erected on any part of the foreshore that is state land allocated to the Ministry of National Development (MND).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: These foreshore structures will not include coastal protection measures as defined in the Sewerage, Drainage and Coastal Protection Act 1999 (SDCPA), as renamed by the Coastal Protection and Other Amendments Act 2026.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Thirdly, BCA will provide administrative support to the Professional Engineers Board and Strata Titles Boards in the performance of their respective statutory functions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Clause 3 amends the Urban Redevelopment Authority Act 1989 to confer the following functions on URA.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: It will also inform and advise the Government on matters relating to the planning of such infrastructure and the planning and implementation of projects to provide and upgrade such infrastructure.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: URA will also provide administrative support to the Board of Architects and the Street and Building Names Board in the performance of their respective statutory functions as well as the Controller of Housing in relation to the administration of the Housing Developers (Control and Licensing) Act 1965 and the Sale of Commercial Properties Act 1979.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: The expanded functions and duties of BCA and URA will enable our agencies to better serve Singaporeans more effectively.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: The second set of amendments provides for the deletion of certain provisions of the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Act 2020 (or COTMA) and related matters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: These COTMA provisions have served their purpose and are no longer required.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Clause 4(b) deletes Part 8C of the COTMA, which provided support to property developers who faced construction delays due to reasons related to COVID-19 and allowed affected purchasers to seek partial reimbursement from the developers for qualifying costs incurred due to the delay in delivery of possession.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Clause 5 provided for saving and transitional provisions to preserve the validity and legal effect of determinations made under Part 8C.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Clause 4(c) deletes Part 10A of the COTMA, which facilitated an equitable co-sharing between contractors and developers of increases in the cost of engaging foreign manpower due to COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Clause 6 is a saving and transitional provision to preserve the validity and legal effect of certain determinations made under Part 10A.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Moving on to Part 4 of the Bill, the fourth set of amendments perform essential legal housekeeping by validating the collection of various fees and charges charged by BCA, the Housing and Development Board (HDB), the National Parks Board (NParks) and URA.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: These include fees for existing operational costs, including for the expedited inspection of buildings and the processing of Temporary Occupation Permits (TOP) by BCA, NParks' animal permits and species certifications, administrative fees charged by HDB and recovery of expenses by HDB and URA for the immobilisation, towage and detention or storage of illegally parked vehicles.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: These fees and charges are essential to recover operational costs incurred by our agencies in providing services to the public.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: When originally introduced, these fees and charges were regarded as administrative charges for specific services or enforcement activities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: However, following a comprehensive internal review, MND was advised that the fees and charges should have been prescribed in legislation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Therefore, clauses 9 to 12 validate fees and charges collected by our Statutory Boards, namely BCA, HDB, NParks and URA in the ordinary course of their operations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: The necessary subsidiary legislation to prescribe the fees has either been made or will be made when this Bill is enacted to provide the agencies with the relevant powers and clear legal basis for the continued collection of these fees.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Clause 13 provides that the validation of the fees and charges made by clauses 9 to 12 do not affect any decision or judgment of the Court given and any Court proceedings commenced before the First Reading of the Bill in relation to the liability of any person to pay any of those fees and charges.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: I will now move on to the last set of amendments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Specifically, clause 16(a) updates definitions regarding "floor area" to reflect the current position set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Clause 15 deletes an amendment to the Building (Strata Management) Act 2004 previously passed in Parliament in 2017 and clause 16(b) to (f) re-enacts that amendment in such a way that it can be brought into force in different stages.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: These pertain to the use of management funds for social and cultural activities, sporting events, engaging legal services or remunerating an official manager where necessary.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: This addresses a practical trade issue where countries may require documentation for artificially propagated plant hybrids even when exempted under Convention of International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) annotations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Including hybrid plants in the definition of "scheduled species" allows NParks to issue the necessary documentation to facilitate trade.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Furthermore, clause 17 empowers the Director-General of Wildlife Trade Control to inspect, analyse and certify both scheduled and non-scheduled species.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: By providing official certification that exported or re-exported products do not contain scheduled species or their parts and derivatives, we provide our legitimate local exporters with the legal certainty they need to meet strict international trade requirements.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Clause 18 amends the Housing and Development Act 1959.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: HDB will be empowered to prescribe fees in respect of anything done by or on behalf of HDB under the Act and the rules made under the Act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Further, the amendments will expressly allow HDB to recover charges and expenses related to the immobilisation, removal and storage of unlawfully parked or abandoned vehicles in HDB common property and open spaces.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: This ensures that the costs of managing such disamenities are borne by the errant owners rather than the public.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: HDB will also be allowed to recover fees, charges, expenses and legal costs incurred in vesting property in the HDB under section 59 of the Act or in compulsorily acquiring property for the reasons listed in section 63(1) of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Maximum fines have been increased for both first-time and repeat offenders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: This will provide stronger deterrence against illegal wildlife feeding and better safeguard public health and safety.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Clause 20 provides for the necessary updates to various Acts arising from the 2020 Revised Edition of Acts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: These amendments collectively strengthen our regulatory framework and ensure our Statutory Boards can continue serving Singaporeans effectively with proper legislative backing.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While their housing contexts differ, their expectations are the same: clear rules, fair enforcement and well-managed living environments.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: My approach to this Bill is guided by a simple principle.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As we expand powers, whether for public agencies or management bodies, we must match them with clarity, fairness and accountability.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While I understand the intent of providing legal certainty, I seek clarification on policy considerations behind these retrospective provisions.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Were there legal gaps that necessitated this approach and how will the Ministry ensure future enforcement actions are firmly grounded in law from the outset?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Retrospective legislation should remain the exception and not the norm.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Those who incurred charges shortly before that date may not have had a reasonable opportunity to seek advice.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I have long supported the EASE programme, and I am glad it is now extended to private estates, because ageing does not discriminate and neither should our policies when it comes to helping seniors age safely.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I also support the clause 16 amendments to the Building (Strata Management) Act.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: First, while access to legal advice is important, there is a risk of increased or prolonged disputes, with costs borne collectively by subsidiary proprietors.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Are safeguards being considered, such as approval thresholds or avenues to challenge unreasonable legal expenditures?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Second, the expanded uses of management funds may strain smaller MCSTs with limited reserves.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How does the Ministry intend to ensure financial prudence and will there be guidance on balancing community activities with long-term sustainability?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Third, as responsibilities expand, council members, many of whom are volunteers, will need greater support.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If mandatory training is introduced, will it include practical guidance on financial management, governance and planning community initiatives?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But as we expand powers, whether for public agencies or MCSTs, we must match them with clarity, safeguards and accountability.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: With these clarifications, I support the Bill and look forward to the Ministry's response.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Today, I will speak four amendments especially relevant to my work in Sengkang.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: First, the empowerment of BCA to administer private estate upgrading programmes; second, increased penalties for wildlife feeding; third, the expansion of scope for MCST management fund utilisation; and finally, HDB's cost recovery for compulsory acquisitions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The maintenance of estate amenities has always ranked high in the list of concerns among both private and public estate residents.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: With respect to this amendment, I would like to raise two specific questions for MND.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Currently, the EASE programme for public estates falls under HDB.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: With BCA now undertaking management of the EASE programme for private estates, I would like to seek clarity on the implementation framework.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: How does BCA plan to partner with MCSTs to implement the installation of fixtures?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Will BCA appoint contractors directly to coordinate installations and maintain quality control across all private estates?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Or will MCSTs retain the discretion to hire their own contractors?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: If the latter, what quality assurance mechanisms will BCA put in place to ensure consistent standards across diverse contractors and estates, given that MCSTs have varying levels of capacity and expertise.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: As the programme is extended to private estates, it is important that robust implementation and quality assurance frameworks are in place to ensure similar positive outcomes.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Second, on post-completion maintenance of the EUP, the same amendment confers on BCA the duty to act as an agent of Government in management, implementation and administration of programmes established and funded by the Government for the upgrading of public spaces, infrastructure and facilities in private estates.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: While the BCA is given a role in consultations and site assessments, the Bill does not clearly address who bears responsibility for estate maintenance and upkeep after upgrading works are done.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I will ask the Ministry to clarify whether this responsibility continues to rest with BCA and if so, whether commensurate support will be extended to them.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Ensuring a fair, transparent and sustainable allocation of resources is critical to the longevity of such programmes.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Over the past year, I have raised several Parliamentary Questions on the management of our pigeon population.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Residents regularly flag concerns about pigeons roosting on aircon ledges, and some even have birds fly into their kitchens and balconies.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I therefore welcome the Bill's stronger stance on wildlife feeding.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: That said, I would urge the Ministry to also address the deeper social dimension of this behaviour.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: A recent CNA article highlighted that the habit of feeding birds can go beyond mere recalcitrance.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: It can reflect social isolation and a lack of purposeful engagement, particularly among seniors.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Penalising behaviour without understanding its root causes risks addressing the symptom while leaving the underlying issue unresolved.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: With this in mind, I would ask the Ministry to consider two complementary measures.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: First, to strengthen partnership with social service agencies to engage residents, especially isolated seniors, on the consequences of wildlife feeding, and to connect them with more meaningful social activities.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Second, to pay the increased penalty regime with a corresponding uplift in enforcement efforts so that the deterrence is not only higher in principle but felt in practice.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: In short, management fund monies may now be applied towards social, cultural, educational and sports activities, as well as engagement of legal services on behalf of the management corporation.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Management funds are, at their core, contributions made collectively by the subsidiary proprietors, residents who trust that their money will be managed prudently and in the interest of the estate.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Any expansion of how these funds can be used, therefore, warrants careful scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Under the current framework, expenditures above a prescribed threshold must be authorised through an ordinary or a special resolution at the annual general meeting, ensuring that residents have a say in significant financial decisions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: If a management corporation wishes to draw on the management fund for a social event or legal engagement, would the existing resolution requirements still govern that decision?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I raise this because the expansion, while bearing good intentions, opens the door to potential misuse if oversight mechanisms are not clearly extended to cover these new categories.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Without clear parametres, there is a risk that funds could be directed towards legal proceedings that serve the interests of a few rather than the collective.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I would ask the Ministry to clarify what safeguards are in place to prevent such outcomes and whether additional disclosure or reporting obligations will accompany this expanded scope.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Getting the safeguards right is just as important as getting the scope right.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: While this represents a small fraction of the broader home ownership population, each case is not merely a statistic, but a family in genuine financial distress.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: In light of this, I would like to pose two questions to MND.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: To prevent abuse, the floor will be activated as long as the Government is satisfied that the family is truly in dire straits through standard evaluation procedures already in place for assessing means.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: My remarks today have centred on four areas of concern: first, the need for a robust implementation framework governing the EUP; second, the increased penalties for wildlife feeding are accompanied by a proportionate social support; third, establishing clear safeguards around the expanded use of MCST management funds; and fourth, securing compassionate support for families facing compulsory acquisition by HDB.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Taken together, these are not merely technical amendments.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I urge the Ministry to address these concerns directly so that the Bill's intentions are realised, not just in letter, but in spirit, delivering outcomes that are fair, sustainable and humane for all.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Hence, I focus my remarks on Part 4, which is of a rather different character.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: When a statutory body has collected fees without the clear rule-making authority to do so, the responsible course is to come to Parliament, put the position right, and ensure that the underlying functions continue on a sound legal footing.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: That said, Mr Speaker, I think this House should take a moment of genuine interest in how we came to need Part 4 at all.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These are not minor agencies charging obscure fees.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Three of them are Statutory Boards with long histories and well-resourced legal and policy functions behind them.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The list of affected collections include some of the most routine transactions a citizen in Singapore will have with the state, paying to expedite a TOP application, paying to register as a renovation contractor, paying a release fee after a vehicle has been clamped in the car park at the foot of one's block.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For each of these fees were being levied and collected over a period that the Bill, itself, implies ran for years on a legal basis that the Government now concedes was inadequate.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: It is a significant thing for this to have happened across four agencies under four different parent Acts, and to have gone undetected for as long as it did.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I would, therefore, like to ask the Minister a few a few questions, because this House and the public deserve clarity.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This is information this House should have before it is asked to put the matter permanently to rest.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Second, on what legal basis did each of these agencies think they had the authority to impose these fees and charges in the first place?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Every one of these validated categories was presumably charged pursuant to something – a rule, a subsidiary instrument, an administrative direction or an internal policy.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: It would assist this House and bolster public confidence in the Bill to understand what the legal basis was in each case and why it was thought at the time to be sufficient?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These are questions about how the relevant agencies arrive at the view of their own powers.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Third, how and when did the Government come to realise that there was a problem?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, what has the Government done to satisfy itself that this problem is confined to four agencies and the categories listed in Part 4?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: A defect of this kind arising across four agencies under four different parent Acts is not the sort of thing one expects to find in isolation.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Is there something specific to the internal processes of these agencies that led to all four of them to independently arrive on a mistaken view of their rule-making authority, or is there a possibility that the rulemaking frameworks of our statutory bodies have a common weakness, which has now been exposed in these four cases, but may still be present in others?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Fifth, has a cross-Government review been commissioned in response to the discovery that led to Part 4?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: If so, who conducted it, what was its scope and over what timeframe?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Are there other agencies, other fee regimes or other categories of collection which the Government has reason to believe may sit on similar uncertain legal foundations?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Should this House expect further validating legislation in future sessions?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The question is beyond primarily formalising existing practice alone, to what extent would it materially expand BCA's ambit and how will BCA's mandate complement rather than overlap with the functions of existing agencies as well as town councils?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: In particular, what gaps or needs were identified that BCA is especially well placed to address, given regulatory and industry-facing expertise?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: More importantly, I also seek clarification on how resident-facing roles will be effectively managed between BCA, Town Councils, agencies and HDB to avoid duplication and redirection.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I also look forward to an update as to how this change will make a difference on the lives of our residents on the ground.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: To what extent can we see increase in efficiency as well as expediency?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Will BCA be increasing its headcount, vendors or contractors, for the agency to be able to keep pace with its expanded functions as well as its key functions, including approving authority for build projects moving ahead?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I will move on next to the enhanced custodial sentencing for feeding wildlife.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: For some Members, they continue to be a mainstay in our appeals and petitions, and top of mind to manage and tackle.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Of course, these amendments to protect public health and safety are critical and much welcome.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: While the enhanced custodial penalty signals the Government is committed to tackling disamenities caused by invasive bird species, it may lead to unintended consequences, especially among seniors and the vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: In the past year, I met several seniors who were fined for feeding pigeons.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: One even built a DIY bird bath at his kitchen ledge, so the birds could have a drink or for when temperatures rise.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: So, awareness is still lacking and education is key.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Many feeders were acting out of habit or compassion, mostly seniors or persons with cognitive impairment.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Could the Senior Parliamentary Secretary please share the Ministry's renewed plans to partner with social service agencies to engage and educate the public, particularly seniors, about the dangers of feeding wild animals ahead of the enforcement?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: While a Member called for a similar move earlier, I also would like to share some concrete examples of intervention that can be considered.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: For example, will the Government consider ramping up efforts to refer cases involving the elderly or cognitively impaired persons to social services agencies for support, including interventions, such as engaging individuals through frequent home visits, counselling, finding alternative activities or interactions with family members or volunteers, so that the offenders would make themselves feel less socially isolated?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I had earlier sought clarification on the expanded role of the BCA, the penalties for feeding wildlife as well as the retrospective validation of fees and charges.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Regarding the BCA, an explanation of how these amendments change the way BCA works with other agencies, such as HDB and Town Councils, would help Singaporeans identify which agency to approach.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: In addition, it is important for the public to understand how BCA will enhance the capacity of its staff and contractors, so as to ensure more efficient implementation, particularly in the approval of building projects.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Meanwhile, on the doubling of penalties for feeding wildlife, I acknowledge that such efforts to protect public health are important and must be given priority.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: However, preparatory measures should also be strengthened, so that the impact on seniors and those with cognitive needs can be addressed.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I recommend an integrated approach – early engagement, education and awareness, as well as collaboration with social service agencies are all important.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: For instance, cases involving seniors or persons with disabilities could be referred through home visits, counselling as well as support in identifying alternative activities.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I also suggest that information be shared openly so that we can collectively review the effectiveness of these amendments.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: What aspects will be strengthened to ensure transparency and understanding?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: That is why explanation, raising awareness, having the right approach and public education are important. : Mr Speaker, this Bill appears to be technical, but it is necessary to understand how provisions will be implemented as they are implications for governance frameworks, coordination between agencies, public confidence as well as awareness.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I am not going to speak on every part of the Bill, but instead, I wish to focus on five specific areas where the amendments directly affect residents' lived experience, professional pathways and public understanding.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The stated aim is to improve the quality of life of residents in those estates.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Very often when we talk about estate upgrading, our mind turns to HDB estates.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And this is understandable because HDB houses about 80% of our resident population.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But ageing in place, mobility and safety, are not only issues faced by people who live in HDB but also many seniors who live in private estates too.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When I visit Faber Hills Estate in my constituency, I meet sizeable number of seniors there.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And this Bill matters to them because it affects their daily living.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This senior shared with me that even as they age, they no longer want to drive.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They want to rely just on their legs.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Therefore, I welcome this Bill, the role that BCA plays in private estates to improve quality of lives.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, I would like to ask the Minister if we could clarify what does quality of life?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: How is it defined in this case, and how do we measure?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Because this phrase sounds simple, but it really can mean different things to different people.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For one resident, quality of life could mean nicer landscaping.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For another, it is better lighting at night.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For an elderly resident, it is about being able to safely walk from the home to the bus stop.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For those on wheelchair and walking aid, it is whether the pavements are even and whether they are safe enough for crossing.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, I hope the Ministry would be able to share what indicators are we looking at to assess quality of life impact and such upgrading works.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Could the Ministry also clarify what does this entail in practice?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For example, does this refer to secretarial support, shared services, case administration, IT system service or operational functions?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This will help us to better understand how this amendment improves efficiency while preserving substantive independence and professional judgement of these bodies.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Administrative support can sound mundane, but it shapes how efficiently and responsively public facing bodies will operate.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If a professional board or tribunal has a good administrative support, applications can be processed faster, correspondence may be clearer and members of public may receive more timely response.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, administrative support should also strengthen efficiency without blurring the roles of relevant boards.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, I appreciate clarification on how BCA support will be structured.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, I would like to talk about URA's expanded role in coordinating transport utilities and other infrastructure planning.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This, in my view, is an important amendment.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, allow me to now return back to the issue of mobility, especially for our seniors.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In my constituency, residents have shared their concerns about overhead bridges not having lifts.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At Faber Hills estate, many residents have been asking for years whether we could build a lift in the overhead bridge linking from Faber Drive to NEWest Park because, honestly, they will prefer just to walk across the bridge to have their breakfast there.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Furthermore, residents have also requested for a lift for the overhead bridge at Block 343 Clementi for more than 10 years.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They say, "David, every time I take a bus, and I stop in front of Block 343 there is a flight of stairs, we just stand there and wait for someone to come and help us to carry our groceries up." These lifts matter to the seniors because they have to climb up a flight of stairs.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, if we are able to build lifts on overhead bridge, this matters to our seniors.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My main point here is this – whether seniors living in private estate or public estate, the need for better infrastructure to support mobility matters to our seniors.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is especially true, as I said, for elderly seniors, residents with mobility issues, parents with prams or caregivers accompanying someone frail.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I appreciate the agencies, such as LTA will continue to lead many of these efforts, but I hope the Minister can clarify how URA's enhanced role will improve coordination and responsiveness to the ground.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Because sometimes the most meaningful infrastructure improvement is not the most dramatic one.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is the one that allows elderly residents to be able to make their journey independently, safely with dignity.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My fourth point concerns recognising pre-qualification of practical experience for architects and professional engineers.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For young people, entering the built environment, the path to professional registration can be a long and demanding one.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is not that after you graduate with an engineering degree, you immediately become a professional engineer.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: That is not true, because it is a long and demanding one today.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Practical experience matter, because their practical experience helped to shape judgement, confidence and professional competency.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If a person has acquired relevant experience before formal qualification, then it is sensible whether this experience should be counted.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is especially important because if we want to attract and retain talent in the built environment sector because many young people want meaningful careers, but they also look at how long the pathway takes and whether the system recognises the work they have already done.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, in principle, I actually support this view and this direction.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, the built environment is also one where public safety is directly at stake.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In my view, the right balance should be this: do not make pathways are unnecessarily long or rigid but also do not make flexibility to become ambiguous.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If pathways are shortened, then public assurance must be strengthened.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My fifth point concerns the inclusion of hybrid plants under endangered species framework.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But I would also like to point out from a practical point of view, from an ordinary consumer, especially those who buy plants online.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Many might not exactly know what a hybrid plant is.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I will be honest to confess to everyone while preparing for this Bill, I also do not understand what exactly a hybrid plant is and I had to Google, "Oh, so this is how a hybrid plant looks like." So, what am I trying to say here?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Many consumers who are just buying plants, they really might not know what constitute a hybrid plant.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, they may not know its origin, whether it is derived from a regulated species.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, I would like to ask the Government – how will the Government ensure that ordinary individuals do not unknowingly break the law?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Will there be public education efforts explaining what kind of plants are affected?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Will there be simple consumer-facing guidance with pictures or examples?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: More broadly, could the Ministry clarify where the responsibility would lie in common scenarios when a consumer buys plant from an online overseas store or a local retailer sells plant without clearly indicating whether it might be a regulated hybrid?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I raise this because strong regulation should go in hand with strong awareness.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I just like to make a brief point on the validation of past fees and charges.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The views validate various fees and charges previously collected by agencies as BCA, HDB, NParks and URA.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In plain English, this means that Parliament is asked to confirm that certain sums collected in the past are to be treated properly and legally collected.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: While I have trust in the integrity of our public servants to do good by Singaporeans, public trust must continue to be sustained and strengthened when such matters are explained clearly and candidly.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As in many views of this nature, the real test is whether the residents will feel the difference if BCA were to take on estate upgrading in our private estate – when our private residential estate residents should feel that their daily mobility, safety and comfort have improved.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If URA is coordinating infrastructure planning, seniors should feel that agencies are working together to solve real access issues on the ground.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If professional pathways are made more flexible, young people should feel that their experience is recognised while the public must remain assured that standards are not diluted.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If hybrid plants are brought in within the regulatory framework, the ordinary consumer should be educated clearly so that compliance is practical and not confusing.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And where past fees and charges are validated, the public should receive clear explanations, so trust is preserved.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have nothing to add on those parts.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My concern is Part 4, the retroactive validation of past fee collections.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Parliament sometimes has to correct administrative mistakes when an agency has been collecting fees without proper legal basis and foundation, and that gap is discovered.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This House may need to regularise that position.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a significant step and Parliament deserves the information to assess whether it is a justified one.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2023, when this House debated the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment No 3) Bill, a Bill to enable President Tharman to hold international appointments in his private capacity with its operative provisions backdated to the date of his inauguration, then Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong stated that "backdating upsets expectations and prejudices individuals who rely on the existing law".

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He went on to argue that backdating in that Bill was acceptable because no one was actually prejudiced.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is one possible test for when retrospective legislation may be appropriate and a reasonable one and it is precisely a test that Parliament cannot apply today because the Government has not told us who was affected by these collections, by how much or for how long.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are being asked to bar citizens from bringing claims without knowing whether those claims have could have had merit.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a second point that the Government needs to address.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the Goods and Services Tax (Amendment) Bill 2024, which addressed wrongly charged Goods and Services Tax (GST) on Government fees, the Government drew a principled line.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The 18 fees were acknowledged as genuinely wrongly charged, collected against its own policy intent were refunded.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fees the Government maintained were correctly charged in substance where the legal basis was uncertain due to inconsistent agency interpretation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Refund for what was wrong in substance validate for what was ambiguous in law.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This House approved that approach and now consider where the agencies referred to in this Bill sit on that spectrum.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They did not merely charge fees on uncertain legal ground, they collected fees and in HDB's case made deductions from acquisition compensation without proper statutory authority.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By the Government's own logic in 2024, that is closer to the category that warrants restitution.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead, Parliament is being asked to validate without refund and without any account of what was taken.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Neither does this House because Government has not said.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are being asked to permanently bar legal proceedings without knowing the claims we are extinguishing.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The HDB compulsory acquisition deductions are where this matters most.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When HDB acquires a resident's flat, the resident is owed compensation as of right.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If HDB was deducting its own administrative and legal costs from that compensation without statutory authority, then affected residents receive less than what the law entitled them to.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those who had already commenced proceedings before 7 April retained their rights, but everyone else is permanently shut out from that date, an arbitrary line drawn at the moment of First Reading.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the deductions were trivial and affected very few people, the Government can say so.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the answer is reassuring, disclosure costs nothing.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will not dwell on this, but it warrants a brief observation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Four Statutory Boards under one Ministry have simultaneously been found to have operated outside of their statutory remit.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It does not explain how this came about across all four agencies at once and it puts no mechanism in place to prevent a recurrence.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, the Bill that we are debating today touches a very fundamental question of fairness.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In simple terms, certain Government agencies have been collecting fees from members of the public without legal authorisation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government now seeks to amend the law to retrospectively legalise these charges and to permanently close the avenue for affected citizens to seek recourse through the Courts.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What concerns me most is that among these unlawful charges are fees deducted by HDB when compulsorily acquiring flats.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As my colleague, Mr Abdul Muhaimin, has pointed out, families facing compulsory acquisition of their homes are often already in very difficult circumstances.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For these families, every cent that has been deducted is money that they can ill-afford to lose.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government owes the public a clear and honest account of what has happened rather than using legislation to quietly draw a line under the matter. : Mr Speaker, the Workers' Party's position is not that administrative lapses can never be retrospectively corrected.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They can, and this House has approved such corrections before.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are the clearer mandates for the BCA and URA, the provisions that enable Government-funded upgrading in private residential estates, and the formal certification framework for endangered species under our environmental laws.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At first glance, these amendments may appear technical and disparate, but taken together, they speak to a deeper responsibility – the duty of stewardship, stewardship of our built environment so that our city remains liveable and humane, stewardship of our neighbourhoods so that no community is left behind as we renew and upgrade, and stewardship of the natural world that our children will inherit.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In a small and highly urbanised country, like Singapore, stewardship is not an abstract ideal.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is a daily discipline of care, planning and restraint.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It requires us to think not just as users of our spaces, but as custodians of what we will pass on to the next generation.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is in this spirit that I support the amendments before us today.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, on the changes to BCA and URA.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Good urban life does not happen by accident.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is the outcome of deliberate planning, careful coordination and the steady work of many public officers whom residents rarely see.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This clarity of mandate is what allows agencies to act decisively instead of passing issues from one agency to another in a way that frustrates the public.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Citizens do not experience the world in terms of which agency is in charge of which function.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They experience whether the footpath is shaded and barrier free, whether the bus stop is sensibly located and whether a new development minimises disruption to daily life.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In a land-scarce city, like Singapore, this kind of integrated planning is essential to our quality of life.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It determines whether an elderly resident can move independently using ramps and lifts, whether a parent pushing a stroller can reach the MRT station without navigating an obstacle course and whether we preserve green spaces as our city becomes denser.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I support these changes because they move us toward a model of urban governance where agencies are empowered to collaborate and to solve problems together.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That is how we make a dense city feel humane, gracious and liveable.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, I support the policies that enable upgrading for private residential estates.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For many years, we have rightly invested in upgrading and renewal for public housing estates.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This has kept older HDB towns liveable and vibrant and it reflects our social compact that public housing should remain a good home throughout a person's life.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, good urban life does not stop at the boundary of an HDB precinct.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many Singaporeans live in older private estates, in walk-up apartments, strata developments or landed homes where common spaces are ageing and accessibility features are lacking.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In some older estates, residents have shared concerns about uneven pavements that are dangerous for seniors or the lack of resting points between bus stops and homes on slopes.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This can support improvements that benefit the wider community, such as accessible paths, safer crossings, greened walkways, better drainage as well as intergenerational fitness and play areas and green spaces where young and old can come together, enjoying enriched social connections and a rejuvenated local community.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Of course, we must design cost sharing, co-creation and citizen consultation arrangements carefully so that homeowners are treated fairly and the voices of tenants, seniors and caregivers are properly heard.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Done well, this is an investment in making every neighbourhood, public or private, a place where people of different ages and abilities can live well together.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, I strongly support the provisions that formalise certification for endangered species and related products.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They carry real responsibility to ensure that our ports, airports and marketplaces do not become conduits for the exploitation of endangered wildlife.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But beyond regulations, we must also confront the profound suffering endured by the trafficked animals.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When animals are trafficked, they are exposed to terrible conditions.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are crammed into carriers with poor ventilation for days if not weeks, with many dying from stress, dehydration and suffocation during transit.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Those that make it into our homes suffer from physical and psychological trauma.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The reptiles with spinal issues from overbreeding and the Indian star tortoises who struggle to adapt to tropical humidity are all examples of the cruelty inflicted on sentient beings if we allow such trade to take place on our shores.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It will help legitimate businesses to prove that their goods are compliant and it helps the authorities to act swiftly and fairly when there is suspicion of illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As markets for exotic plants, animals and derivatives become more complex with hybrids, online trading and niche collectors, we cannot rely on outdated or vague definitions.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can we aspire to be a city that prospers while setting high standards for environmental stewardship?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: By tightening our endangered species regime and making certification more robust, we signal that Singapore chooses to acknowledge the incredibly hidden but rich native biodiversity.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our precious and sensitive ecosystems support some of the rarest species on Earth – the Sunda pangolin, Singapore freshwater crab and straw-headed bulbul.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Each illegally trafficked animal carries more than suffering on the individual level, but the potential to change our natural habitats and change our biodiversity and landscape forever.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must instead strive to upkeep the gentle balance of our natural world so that our children and many more after them may continue to marvel at natural wonder and the wisdom it brings to our society.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Last but not least, I would like to speak on the amendments made to the Wildlife Act 1965 with regard to wildlife feeding.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But more importantly, they also reflect a growing understanding that not all harms to wildlife come from malice.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When residents feed pigeons and crows in our parks and public spaces, they often do so out of genuine compassion and love for animals.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, these birds are remarkably well adapted to urban life and are fully capable of foraging for their own food.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In fact, it has been observed that pigeons often forage for food on open fields if they are not given human food.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Artificial feeding can disrupt the ecosystem, leading to increased competition with native birds and eventually culling in massive numbers when populations start to affect our human environment.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The cruelty is beyond the feeding and culling, but the cascade of consequences onto our native wildlife and neighbours due to our actions.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This amendment hopefully invites us to reflect more broadly on our relationship with the way we view urban wildlife.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are these animals that we complain about encroaching into our spaces or have we rather encroached into theirs?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Who truly belongs where and what does genuine co-existence look like?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can we truly be a city in nature if our greenery is sterile, quiet and homogenous?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need more serious, ongoing conversations in our spaces.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must learn that kindness takes many forms and sometimes restraint is compassion and consideration.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some may have noticed some banners that we have recently put up in Bishan East-Sin Ming trying to address these issues, with poems written in four languages reminding people that the truly kind act is not to feed the birds as they are able to forage for food on their own.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some described the posters as Shakespeare in the Wild.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But moving forwards requires not just poetic words but deep conviction and a willingness to change our attitudes and behaviours to understand that protecting wildlife often means stepping back and allowing wild animals to remain wild instead of feeding them.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Only when we can peacefully co-exist with our wild neighbours can we honour our urban environments.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That said, I would like to put forth some clarifications about the amendments within this Bill.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, on the changes of scope to the URA and BCA Act.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How will the enhanced statutory coordinating role of URA interact with existing planning functions of agencies, like LTA, HDB and PUB, and what mechanisms will be used to resolve disagreements in priorities or timelines?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could the Government provide clearer criteria or examples of the types of projects where URA will now take the lead in coordination, versus where sectoral agencies remain the primary drivers?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On the amendments pertaining to upgrading of private estates, what are the key criteria that will be used to identify which private residential estates can benefit from Government-funded upgrading and will there be a transparent application or nomination process?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How will the Government ensure that less well-off or older private estates, which may have weaker management corporations or more vulnerable residents, are not left behind compared to more organised and better-resourced estates?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What types of works will be prioritised under these upgrading programmes, for example barrier free access, safety features, environmental sustainability or amenities and how will trade-offs be decided?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How does the Government intend to maintain a fair balance between long-standing commitments to HDB upgrading and the extension of support to private estates, so that perceptions of equity are preserved?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will there be phased implementation, grace periods or targeted support, for example, guidance materials or clinics, to help smaller players adapt to the new certification regime?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While the amended penalties under the Wildlife Act serve as important financial deterrents, we must recognise that many bird feeders act out of genuine kindness.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For many elderly seniors, feeding birds provides purpose, connection and dignity.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Rather than only punishing this expression of unmet need, should we not address the loneliness itself through befriending programmes and community services?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Please allow me to address Members' comments in six broad areas.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: The first area is on the expanded functions and duties of the BCA and URA.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Mr David Hoe asked about URA's expanded coordinating role and how it will interact with existing planning functions of agencies, like LTA, HDB and PUB.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: First, let me clarify that URA already coordinates infrastructure and land use planning as part of its role as Singapore's national urban planning authority.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: URA works with different agencies through existing inter-agency platforms and administrative processes to ensure that infrastructure is implemented ahead of time.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: These are large-scale infrastructure which are planned and implemented to support developments, such as industries, public housing and transport facilities and train lines.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: The amendments do not supersede the primary planning responsibilities and functions of agencies, like LTA and HDB.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: These agencies will continue to lead planning and implementation of their development and infrastructure within their respective domains, such as for smaller-scale, municipal infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: For instance, to Mr David Hoe's query, the retrofitting of lifts in overhead bridges will continue to be led by LTA.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Agencies will continue to work together to resolve issues which require cross-agency collaboration.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: With regard to BCA's expanded functions in managing upgrading programmes in private residential estates, Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim asked about how BCA's role will complement that of other agencies, as well as about the resourcing for BCA.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Mr David Hoe asked about the criteria for selecting private estates for upgrading, how works are prioritised and coordinated and how their impact is measured.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: The respective roles of other agencies, such as HDB and NParks, remain unchanged.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: When needed, BCA will work with agencies to coordinate upgrading works, as well as engagements with residents.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: And on resourcing, we will resource BCA as necessary to carry out its functions.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Private residential estates are selected for upgrading based on a range of factors.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: For instance, under the EUP which enhances the publicly accessible common areas in private estates, MND considers factors, such as the estates' age and physical condition, the urgency of works needed and whether there is meaningful scope for improvement.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: The prioritisation of upgrading works is based on the specific conditions and needs of each estate, with a focus on improvements that directly enhance residents' safety, accessibility and liveability.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: To Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik's question about the maintenance and upkeep of the completed works in EUP, the maintenance of upgraded infrastructure and facilities is undertaken by the respective agencies, such as NParks and LTA.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: A resident-centred approach is adopted for the evaluation of upgrading works, to assess whether the upgrades make a meaningful difference to residents' daily lives.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: For example, under the recently launched EASE (Private) programme, BCA has introduced a post-installation feedback process to seek residents' views on their satisfaction with the application and installation process and to identify areas for improvement.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: After installation, the owners or occupants would be responsible for the maintenance of the fittings.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: We have announced the details of the programme in February 2026 and the Member may wish to refer to the details of the programme on the EASE (Private) website.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Mr David Hoe also asked about the nature of BCA's administrative support to the Professional Engineers Board and the Strata Titles Boards, and the governance arrangements which will be put in place to ensure that the independence and judgement of the Boards is preserved.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: I wish to assure the Member that BCA's role is strictly administrative.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: BCA provides routine back-office administrative support to the Professional Engineers Board Singapore and the Strata Titles Boards, such as in book-keeping and payroll processing.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: All regulatory, decision-making and adjudicative functions remain solely with the respective Boards.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: These arrangements allow the Boards to focus on their core functions, while benefiting from BCA's sectoral expertise and the economies of scale from shared administrative resources.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: The next area is on the recognition of pre-qualification experience for professional engineers and architects.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Mr David Hoe asked whether recognition of pre-qualification experience might dilute professional standards.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: To be clear, this set of amendments allow the Professional Engineers Board and the Board of Architects to consider recognising relevant pre-qualification experience.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Before doing so, the Boards will assess whether the pre-qualification practical experience is relevant and adequately contributes to candidates developing the competencies and skills expected of a professional engineer or registered architect.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: The third theme of questions surround the validation of fees collected by MND's Statutory Boards, which Mr David Hoe, Ms Valerie Lee, Mr Fadli Fawzi, Mr Andre Low and Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim raised.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: The fees and charges in question were introduced over the years by various Statutory Boards for the provision of specific services to support residents' and industry's needs.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: I wish to assure Mr David Hoe that the fees were appropriate and charged in good faith for services that were duly provided, based on the principles of cost recovery.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: We also disagree with how Mr Andre Low and Mr Fadli Fawzi have characterised the issue.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: MND has chosen to bring this issue to Parliament as we are open and transparent about the matter.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Mr Andre Low also mentioned that 18 fees were acknowledged as genuinely wrongly charged, collected against policy intent and were subsequently refunded as part of the Goods and Services Tax (Amendment) Bill in 2024.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: However, in those cases, only the GST was refunded and not the actual fee itself, as they were collected in line with policy intent.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: In the specific case of compulsory acquisition by the HDB, GST was not charged as part of the fees, and the fees were also collected in line with policy intent.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: To Mr Muhaimin's point on compulsory acquisition of HDB flats, compulsory acquisition cases are assessed on a case-by-case basis, and some cases are not just due to mortgage arrears, but are due to the violation of the HDB lease, such as renting out the entire flat during the minimum occupation period.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: The cut-off date of 7 April 2026 is the date of the First Reading of the Bill.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: If the Bill is passed, legal proceedings with respect of the collection or payment of the fees will be prevented from being instituted between the First Reading and the date which the Bill comes into force.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: This approach aligns to that for validations under previous Bills, such as the Transport Sector (Miscellaneous Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: None of the validated fees were previously subject to legal challenge or adverse judicial comment.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Moving forward, the agencies will assess if new fees or charges being introduced are related to the carrying out of statutory or regulatory functions and properly prescribe them in legislation if needed.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Fourthly, Mr David Hoe has asked about how the Government will ensure that ordinary individuals do not unknowingly break the law under the expanded endangered species framework.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Information is available on the NParks' website and members of the public are welcome to reach out to NParks for clarity on whether permits or certificates are needed.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: On the amendments to the Wildlife Act, Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim and Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik asked about the Government's plans to educate the public about the impact of feeding wildlife and partnership with social service agencies, particularly for seniors.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Ms Elysa Chen asked whether the Government would consider alternative penalties for repeat bird-feeding offenders, given that some offenders are seniors whose behaviour is linked to loneliness and a need for social support.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: As repeat offences will no longer be punishable only with a fine, the Court will have other sentencing options under the Criminal Procedure Code 2010, including community-based orders, such as mandatory treatment orders.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: To Mr Abdul Muhaimin's question, NParks will continue to partner agencies, such as the People's Association and Town Councils, on enforcement and surveillance efforts to deter illegal wildlife feeding.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: We do need appropriate penalties to deter errant behaviours, but our approach is not merely to penalise.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: NParks will continue its public education efforts and partner with the Agency for Integrated Care, Town Councils and other agencies to engage elderly offenders and those with mental health or psychological needs, to understand their underlying needs and motivations that drive such behaviour to address misconceptions and to raise awareness on the negative impacts of bird feeding.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: NParks offers feeders with mental health needs nature-based activities, like community gardening and bird watching, as alternatives to feeding.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: To Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim's question on whether the Government would publish data on illegal bird-feeding, we have previously shared data with this House and will continue to do so where appropriate.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Moving on to other miscellaneous amendments, Member Ms Valerie Lee asked about the use of management funds of MCST.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: I seek the House's full support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: To begin with, I would like to clearly frame my concern with the Bill.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: Against this, we also have no idea about the size of the people who are affected.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: We also do not know the quantum affected.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: Are we talking about hundreds of thousands, or hundreds of millions of dollars?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: So, I hope the Ministry can understand why there is this deep concern with me, especially since as I have said before, these are not obscure transactions, but routine transactions which affect a huge number of people, a huge number of citizens of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: How many Singaporeans have been affected by these collections?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: And I think it is important to know this information before we decide on this matter.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: The other thing that sort of makes me apprehensive is that, on what legal basis did each of the agencies think that they had authority to impose these fees and charges?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: Because if I am not wrong, the Senior Parliamentary Secretary said that it was classified under administrative fees.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: But what was the legal basis of enabling them or allowing them to understand that they were allowed to charge these administrative fees?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
